Overview and definitions
Healthcare equity aims to eliminate avoidable differences in health and health care across population groups defined by race/ethnicity, socioeconomic status, geography, disability, language, and other social identities. Interventions that promote equity address both social and structural determinants, improve access and quality of care, and monitor within-group gaps as outcomes rather than only aggregate improvements. <cite id="ac5e239a-0">The underperformance of the U.S. system in equity and value relative to peer countries underscores the need for targeted interventions for disadvantaged groups, including racial and ethnic minorities, refugees, and low-income populations</cite> <cite id="ac5e239a-0">Interventions mapping to community engagement and outreach, culturally-tailored care, technology adoption, and policy reforms have shown critical roles for community health workers and culturally responsive programs</cite>. <cite id="ac5e239a-4">However, many interventions measure total population outcomes rather than changes in gaps between groups, and system accountability and structural change are needed</cite>.

Strategy categories with mechanisms and evidence

1) Community-based care and community health workers (CHWs)
Mechanism: Social support, navigation, coordination, culturally concordant counseling, and addressing social determinants link marginalized populations to care and community resources. <cite id="0270ba80-1">In the U.S., CHWs target communities experiencing structural oppression—Black, Latine, American Indian/Alaska Native, and Asian/Pacific Islander populations, as well as rural and low-income communities—and improve access, cultural and linguistic competence, and health outcomes by addressing social and structural determinants</cite>. <cite id="0270ba80-1">Evidence reviews and policy analyses describe CHW integration models into health and public health systems and summarize impacts on population health, patient experience, costs, and measures of health equity</cite>.

Effectiveness examples: <cite id="ac5e239a-0">Across 54 systematic reviews synthesized in an umbrella review, CHWs and culturally responsive programs consistently improved access and outcomes for disadvantaged groups</cite>. <cite id="0270ba80-3">A Navajo diabetes program linking clinic providers, CHRs, and patients improved glycated hemoglobin and patient-reported health, illustrating multilevel CHW integration benefits</cite>. <cite id="ac5e239a-0">Evidence also highlights CHWs’ role in enhancing preventive care, particularly cancer screenings among racial and ethnic minority groups</cite>. <cite id="0270ba80-4">At the same time, gaps persist in sustainable implementation and payment models that adequately reimburse CHWs, a barrier to scale</cite>.

Implementation notes: <cite id="0270ba80-0">Social and cultural alignment of CHWs with served populations is crucial, and evidence from other chronic disease areas suggests similar benefits for sickle cell disease by addressing access, care delivery, and cultural mismatch barriers</cite>. <cite id="ac5e239a-4">Umbrella-level guidance emphasizes moving beyond grant-funded pilots to sustained policies and interventions that explicitly reduce gaps between groups</cite>.

2) Culturally tailored and linguistically responsive care
Mechanism: Matching providers, materials, and practices to patients’ cultural identities and languages improves trust, communication, appropriateness of care, and adherence. <cite id="ac5e239a-0">Culturally-tailored interventions and language-concordant care emerged as high-leverage strategies in U.S. evidence syntheses</cite>. <cite id="0270ba80-1">CHW-led navigation and coaching function as culturally grounded implementation supports that enhance equity</cite>.

Effectiveness: <cite id="ac5e239a-0">Systematic reviews report improved access to care and health outcomes for minority and Indigenous communities when interventions are culturally tailored and community partnered</cite>. <cite id="ac5e239a-4">Despite these gains, few studies explicitly measure reductions in inequity gaps, indicating a need for equity-focused evaluation designs</cite>.

3) Digital and delivery innovations (telehealth, mobile clinics)
Mechanism: Extend access across geography and time; integrate outreach, reminders, and follow-up to close utilization gaps. <cite id="ac5e239a-0">Technology adoption—digital health tools and telehealth—are established intervention themes in equity-focused reviews</cite>. <cite id="ac5e239a-3">In marginalized pediatric populations, integrated initiatives combining outreach, telemedicine, mobile clinics, and preventive campaigns significantly improved utilization, treatment access, vaccination coverage, and preventive engagement, with an integrated equity framework scoring highest in effectiveness</cite>.

Implementation notes: <cite id="ac5e239a-0">Programs that pair digital tools with community engagement and culturally responsive practices show stronger and more durable gains than technology alone</cite>. <cite id="ac5e239a-4">Evidence gaps remain on measuring gap-closure between groups and sustaining models financially</cite>.

4) Social determinants of health (SDOH) interventions
Mechanism: Address housing instability, transportation barriers, food insecurity, and safety through partnerships to move from episodic care to upstream risk reduction. <cite id="ac5e239a-0">Umbrella evidence frames disparities as preventable and unjust, linking disease presentation, care delivery, and outcomes to social and structural determinants</cite>. <cite id="ac5e239a-2">The American Society of Hematology Health Equity Compendium illustrates SDOH-driven disparities across conditions and the need for cross-sector, equity-focused research and practice</cite>.

Effectiveness: <cite id="0270ba80-1">In high-income settings, CHWs and public health partnerships improve well-being by addressing SDOH and structural determinants, often exerting larger effects than clinical care alone</cite>. <cite id="ac5e239a-3">Mobile outreach and telehealth reduce structural barriers for families, improving preventive engagement</cite>. <cite id="ac5e239a-0">Population-level syntheses emphasize that interventions should directly target SDOH barriers where inequities concentrate</cite>.

5) Policy and financing levers (single-payer/coverage expansion, targeted investments)
Mechanism: Expand eligibility and financial protection to reduce unmet need and delay/foregone care; fund safety-net capacity; create payers/incentives that reward equitable performance.
- Coverage expansion: <cite id="4fbcaa20-0">A quasi-experimental difference-in-differences analysis using NHIS data (2010–2016) found Medicaid expansion significantly decreased uninsured rates and increased Medicaid coverage across racial/ethnic groups; disparities in delayed care and unmet need narrowed, though overall disparities were not significantly reduced</cite>. <cite id="4fbcaa20-2">Systematic and narrative reviews show Hispanic adult uninsured rates fell from 32% to 12% in expansion vs. non-expansion states by 2016, with persistent higher uninsured rates in non-expansion states for Black and Hispanic adults; minorities in non-expansion states are more likely to delay or forego care, contributing to higher preventable hospitalizations</cite>. <cite id="4fbcaa20-3">State-specific analyses indicate uneven distribution of ACA benefits across states, with limited changes in racial coverage disparities and continuing higher uninsured rates for Black adults, especially in non-expansion “coverage gap” states where people of color comprise a large share</cite>.
- Equity-focused payment and accountability: <cite id="ac5e239a-4">Equality improvement projects (EQIPs) propose pay-for-equity schemes that require systematic collection and reporting of outcomes by targeted demographics over time, leveraging multidisciplinary teams, staff education, and continuous outcome tracking tools to evaluate progress toward gaps between groups</cite>. <cite id="ac5e239a-1">A scoping review of 40 EQIPs found most efforts targeted race/ethnicity disparities, often in primary and outpatient settings, with documented interventions and follow-up audits relatively scarce</cite>.
- Structural racism mitigation: <cite id="4fbcaa20-3">Where states have not expanded Medicaid, structural racism persists in coverage gaps affecting predominantly African American populations in the coverage gap, underscoring that policy decisions themselves can embed inequities that require explicit mitigation</cite>. <cite id="4fbcaa20-4">Scoping reviews of Medicaid expansion’s effects report mixed evidence on disparities in utilization and treatment, with some reductions in maternal mortality and limited changes in broader health status, indicating coverage expansion is necessary but not sufficient for full equity</cite>.

Implementation frameworks and accountability

- Equality improvement projects (EQIPs): <cite id="ac5e239a-4">EQIPs formalize a shift from quality improvement to equity-focused improvement by setting standards for identifying disparities, implementing tailored interventions, and continuously monitoring outcomes by demographic subgroup to evaluate adherence and progress</cite>. <cite id="ac5e239a-1">Lessons from 40 studies emphasize institutional roots, primary care settings, and a focus on race/ethnicity disparities, with half of studies leveraging multidisciplinary teams and continuous tracking</cite>.
- Equity impact assessment and measurement: <cite id="ac5e239a-4">Umbrella reviews call for system accountability, explicit measurement of within-group gaps, and development of new care models</cite>. <cite id="4fbcaa20-0">Using the National Academy of Medicine’s disparity framework, analyses should distinguish changes in absolute gap sizes and not rely solely on proportional changes or aggregate improvements</cite>.
- Community partnerships and culturally responsive delivery: <cite id="ac5e239a-0">Community engagement and partnerships with CHWs are central to improving outcomes for minority and Indigenous populations</cite>. <cite id="0270ba80-0">Cultural alignment and social support are core to CHW effectiveness across chronic conditions</cite>.
- Integration and sustainability: <cite id="0270ba80-4">Critical gaps remain in implementation and sustainment strategies, including payer policies that adequately pay CHWs to function “at the top of license,” which constrains scale and continuity</cite>.

Cross-cutting barriers and enablers

Barriers:
- Financing and reimbursement: <cite id="0270ba80-4">Lack of sustainable payment models for CHWs and equity-focused services</cite>; <cite id="4fbcaa20-3">structural coverage gaps and uneven ACA diffusion across states</cite>.
- Measurement and accountability: <cite id="ac5e239a-0">Most interventions measure total population outcomes rather than explicit gap-closure between groups</cite>; <cite id="ac5e239a-4">few programs implement continuous tracking by subgroup, impeding accountability</cite>.
- Structural determinants: <cite id="0270ba80-1">SDOH and cultural norms shape access and outcomes, requiring cross-sector action beyond clinical settings</cite>.

Enablers:
- Political and payer commitment: <cite id="4fbcaa20-0">Medicaid expansion demonstrates that broad financial protection can reduce uninsured status and specific access disparities, especially for delayed care and unmet need</cite>.
- Community trust and navigation: <cite id="ac5e239a-0">Community partnerships and CHWs enhance cultural and linguistic competence and close utilization gaps</cite>.
- Multidisciplinary integration: <cite id="ac5e239a-1">EQIPs that improve equity leverage multidisciplinary expertise, staff education, and continuous tools to track outcomes</cite>.

Practical strategies to implement and scale

- Expand coverage and close structural gaps: <cite id="4fbcaa20-0">Adopt coverage expansion models (e.g., Medicaid eligibility up to 138% FPL) to lower uninsurance and unmet need across groups and narrow delays in care</cite>; <cite id="4fbcaa20-2">prioritize expansion in non-expansion states where Hispanic and Black adult uninsured rates remain double those in expansion states and cost-related foregone care is common</cite>; <cite id="4fbcaa20-3">eliminate coverage gaps that disproportionately affect people of color</cite>.
- Build and fund an equitable CHW workforce: <cite id="0270ba80-1">Integrate CHWs into clinics and public health with roles in navigation, coaching, and advocacy; pay for advanced functions and sustained case management to enable gap-closure</cite>; <cite id="0270ba80-3">deploy multilevel partnerships (providers, CHRs, patients) for chronic disease management with measurable clinical improvements</cite>.
- Embed cultural and linguistic tailoring: <cite id="ac5e239a-0">Design services for language-concordant care and culturally responsive workflows, co-developed with affected communities</cite>; <cite id="0270ba80-0">ensure CHW cultural alignment and social support as core mechanisms</cite>.
- Tackle SDOH with cross-sector partnerships: <cite id="ac5e239a-2">Coordinate with housing, transportation, food, and social services; apply the SDOH lens to disease presentation and outcomes</cite>; <cite id="0270ba80-1">use CHW outreach to address structural determinants that outweigh clinical care in influencing health</cite>.
- Deploy digital inclusion with equity guardrails: <cite id="ac5e239a-3">Combine telehealth, mobile clinics, and outreach for marginalized families to raise preventive engagement and vaccination rates</cite>; <cite id="ac5e239a-0">pair technology with community engagement and culturally tailored content to avoid digital divide amplification</cite>.
- Institutionalize equity measurement and improvement: <cite id="ac5e239a-4">Adopt EQIPs: define disparities, implement interventions, and track subgroup outcomes over time; consider pay-for-equity structures tied to documented reductions in inequity gaps</cite>; <cite id="4fbcaa20-0">use NAM’s disparity framework to quantify gap changes in access and treatment</cite>; <cite id="ac5e239a-1">conduct equity audits and follow-up assessments to ensure sustained impact</cite>.

What works, for whom, and in what contexts

- CHW-led community integration improves access and clinical outcomes in minority and Indigenous populations when services are culturally aligned and integrated with providers. <cite id="ac5e239a-0">Evidence across chronic conditions and preventive services indicates improved access and outcomes, especially for underserved groups</cite> <cite id="0270ba80-3">and Navajo diabetes programs demonstrate HbA1c and self-reported health gains through multilevel partnerships</cite>.
- Coverage expansion reduces financial barriers and improves preventive utilization, with the strongest effects in states that expanded Medicaid and in populations historically without coverage. <cite id="4fbcaa20-0">Analyses show significant decreases in uninsurance and improvements in access measures, with narrowing of delays and unmet need gaps</cite> <cite id="4fbcaa20-2">Hispanic adult uninsured rates dropped from 32% to 12% in expansion vs. non-expansion states by 2016</cite>. <cite id="4fbcaa20-4">However, many outcome and treatment disparities persist or show limited change, indicating coverage is necessary but not sufficient</cite>.
- Equity measurement remains a bottleneck. <cite id="ac5e239a-0">Most studies evaluate total population improvements rather than within-group gaps, and research-to-policy translation is limited</cite>. <cite id="ac5e239a-4">EQIPs and pay-for-equity proposals can close this gap by mandating subgroup reporting and continuous tracking</cite>.

Unanswered questions and research needs
- Effectiveness of AI and algorithmic tools in reducing bias and improving equitable triage, diagnosis, and care coordination requires rigorous audits and prospective studies. <cite id="ac5e239a-0">Umbrella reviews highlight the need for system accountability and structural inequity interventions but provide limited direct evidence on AI bias mitigation</cite>.
- Sustained financing for CHW programs and community partnerships at scale. <cite id="0270ba80-4">Payment models that allow CHWs to function at the top of license and sustain interventions are underdeveloped in high-income settings</cite>.
- Health and health equity effects of telehealth expansion when paired with broadband access and culturally tailored content. <cite id="ac5e239a-3">Programmatic evidence shows utilization and preventive gains</cite>, but large-scale studies quantifying gap-closure across racial/ethnic groups and rural populations are needed. <cite id="ac5e239a-0">Integrating equity metrics into technology evaluations is a recognized gap</cite>.

Pragmatic roadmap for systems
1) Define equity goals and disparities: adopt NAM-aligned disparity frameworks and establish subgroup-specific dashboards for access, utilization, quality, and outcomes. <cite id="4fbcaa20-0">Use gap metrics (e.g., absolute differences in delayed care and unmet need) to track closure</cite>.
2) Close structural gaps in financial protection: expand eligibility and eliminate coverage gaps; prioritize safety-net capacity in underserved communities. <cite id="4fbcaa20-2">Coverage expansion narrows racial/ethnic uninsured and access disparities</cite>; <cite id="4fbcaa20-3">eliminate the Medicaid coverage gap to mitigate structural racism</cite>.
3) Build an equitable workforce and infrastructure: fund and integrate CHWs and culturally tailored services across primary care, public health, and community-based settings; ensure language access and transportation supports. <cite id="0270ba80-1">CHWs address SDOH and access barriers in marginalized communities</cite> <cite id="ac5e239a-0">and improve preventive care delivery</cite>.
4) Invest in SDOH interventions and digital inclusion: form cross-sector partnerships to address housing, food, and transportation; deploy telehealth and mobile outreach with equity guardrails to avoid exacerbating digital divides. <cite id="ac5e239a-3">Integrated outreach, telemedicine, and mobile clinics improved preventive engagement and vaccinations</cite>.
5) Institutionalize equity improvement: implement EQIPs with defined interventions, timelines, and pay-for-equity incentives tied to subgroup gap reductions; commit to continuous equity audits and public reporting. <cite id="ac5e239a-4">EQIPs leverage multidisciplinary teams and continuous outcome tracking to move from quality to equality improvement</cite> <cite id="ac5e239a-1">and emphasize follow-up audits to verify sustained disparity reduction</cite>.

Summary
Equity-improving strategies converge on expanding financial protection, building culturally aligned community-based workforces, addressing SDOH, and embedding equity measurement and accountability into organizational and payer policies. <cite id="ac5e239a-0">Community engagement, culturally tailored care, technology adoption, and policy reforms—especially Medicaid expansion—have demonstrated measurable effects on access and specific disparities</cite>. <cite id="ac5e239a-4">However, systems must shift from aggregate gains to explicit gap-closure by adopting EQIPs, pay-for-equity incentives, and continuous subgroup monitoring</cite>. <cite id="4fbcaa20-4">Where coverage expansion alone shows limited changes in some outcomes, targeted SDOH and community-integrated models are needed to translate protection into improved health status and reduced inequities</cite>. <cite id="0270ba80-4">Sustained success hinges on payment models that enable CHWs and community partnerships to function at full scope and on leadership committed to structural change</cite>.

Title: Advancing equity and value in United States healthcare: an umbrella review
Snippet: Background The United States (U.S.) healthcare system consistently underperforms in equity and value compared to peer countries. Socially disadvantaged groups, such as racial and ethnic minorities, refugees, and low-income populations, experience worse access to healthcare and poorer health outcomes. This issue highlights the need for targeted interventions to reduce disparities and improve healthcare quality in both public health and clinical practice. This scoping review aims to map existing literature on interventions that promote healthcare equity and value in the US, focusing on access to healthcare and health outcomes for disadvantaged populations. Methods A scoping review of systematic reviews was conducted to map literature on high-value, equitable healthcare in the U.S. Using the Arksey and O’Malley framework and PRISMA-ScR guidelines, the review focused on systematic reviews of interventions, strategies, and policies promoting healthcare equity and value published between 2018 and 2023 that addressed U.S.-based healthcare. A two-step article selection process and qualitative synthesis of findings were employed. Results The review synthesized 54 studies, comprising mostly systematic reviews, scoping reviews, and meta-analyses. These studies focused on disadvantaged populations, including racial and ethnic minorities, refugees, and low-income groups. Interventions were categorized into four themes: community engagement and outreach (e.g., use of community health workers), culturally-tailored interventions (e.g., language-concordant care), technology adoption (e.g., digital health tools), and policy reforms (e.g., Medicaid expansion). Findings highlighted the critical role of community health workers and culturally responsive programs in improving access to care and health outcomes for disadvantaged populations. However, most interventions, including these approaches, aim to improve health outcomes measured across whole populations, rather than healthcare gaps between groups within populations. Conclusions This review underscores the importance of culturally tailored interventions, community engagement and outreach, and policy reforms in addressing equity and value in healthcare. There is a significant gap in research directly tackling healthcare inequities. Future research should focus on system accountability, addressing structural inequities, and developing new care models to enhance equity and value. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12939-026-02784-4.

Title: Community Health Workers as Support for Sickle Cell Care
Snippet: Community health workers are increasingly recognized as useful for improving health care and health outcomes for a variety of chronic conditions. Community health workers can provide social support, navigation of health systems and resources, and lay counseling. Social and cultural alignment of community health workers with the population they serve is an important aspect of community health worker intervention. Although community health worker interventions have been shown to improve patient-centered outcomes in underserved communities, these interventions have not been evaluated with sickle cell disease. Evidence from other disease areas suggests that community health worker intervention also would be effective for these patients. Sickle cell disease is complex, with a range of barriers to multifaceted care needs at the individual, family/friend, clinical organization, and community levels. Care delivery is complicated by disparities in health care: access, delivery, services, and cultural mismatches between providers and families. Current practices inadequately address or provide incomplete control of symptoms, especially pain, resulting in decreased quality of life and high medical expense. The authors propose that care and care outcomes for people with sickle cell disease could be improved through community health worker case management, social support, and health system navigation. This report outlines implementation strategies in current use to test community health workers for sickle cell disease management in a variety of settings. National medical and advocacy efforts to develop the community health workforce for sickle cell disease management may enhance the progress and development of “best practices” for this area of community-based care.
</snippet>

Title: Community Health Worker Integration with and Effectiveness in Health Care and Public Health in the United States.
Snippet: Community health workers (CHWs) are increasingly recognized as an essential part of the health workforce globally, and their presence has been growing steadily in high-income countries including the United States (92). In low-and middle-income countries, CHWs expand access to scarce health care resources. In higher-income countries, CHWs work to improve overall health in under-resourced communities by providing social support, care coordination, navigation, coaching, and advocacy. Despite having the highest per capita spending on health care of any country, the United States has poor health and health care outcomes relative to other high-income countries (117). The United States is also home to stark health inequities, which are driven largely by social determinants of health (SDOH)-the conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work, and age-and by structural determinants of health-cultural norms, policies, and practices that define the often inequitable distribution of SDOH (21,79). In the United States, the majority of CHWs serve communities that have experienced structural oppression and who are marginalized by traditional health care systems, including Black, Latine, American Indian/Alaska Native, and Asian/Pacific Islander communities, as well as rural and low-income communities (15,52). CHWs provide a critical link between these communities and the health care and public health services they need, improving access to care, cultural and linguistic competence of care, and health outcomes. Moreover, CHWs can improve well-being by addressing social and structural determinants of health, which often play a greater role in health outcomes than health care does (20). As the United States increases investments in the CHW workforce, it is important to understand the current state of evidence regarding CHW effectiveness in health care, public health, and community-based settings. 

This article builds on a 2014 review (92) to summarize current evidence related to the integration of CHWs into health care and public health services and their effectiveness in the United States. Healthcare equity aims to eliminate avoidable differences in health and health care across population groups defined by race/ethnicity, socioeconomic status, geography, disability, language, and other social identities. Title: Community Health Workers as Support for Sickle Cell Care
Snippet: Community health workers are increasingly recognized as useful for improving health care and health outcomes for a variety of chronic conditions. Title: Community Health Worker Integration with and Effectiveness in Health Care and Public Health in the United States.
Snippet: Community health workers (CHWs) are increasingly recognized as an essential part of the health workforce globally, and their presence has been growing steadily in high-income countries including the United States (92). We provide a brief history of CHW integration with health care in the United States, describe models of health care integration, and review and assess the evidence regarding the impact of CHW programs on population health, patients' experience of health care, health care costs, and measures of health equity.

This scoping review reinforces the importance of community partnerships, especially the involvement of CHWs, in improving health outcomes for underserved populations. Our findings also reinforce earlier studies that emphasized the effectiveness of CHWs in enhancing preventive care, particularly cancer screenings among racial and ethnic minority groups [67]. Despite the breadth of interventions identified in the included reviews, a notable gap existed in the extent to which these reviews examined interventions that explicitly measured or targeted reductions in inequities (i.e., changes in gaps between groups), rather than improvements within disadvantaged populations. A National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (NASEM) committee reviewed racial and ethnic disparities in healthcare from 2003 to 2022 and concluded in their report, "Ending Unequal Treatment, " that these disparities persist with little overall improvement [69]. There is a striking gap between the large scope and scale of these disparities across disease conditions and the continuum of care, and the comparatively few interventions to address them. Many reviews assessed improvements in healthcare outcomes for disadvantaged groups without fully considering whether the interventions successfully reduced disparities. This points to a significant research gap, as interventions need to move beyond grant-funded interventions for socially disadvantaged groups to implementing sustained policies, strategies, and interventions that address longstanding inequities in healthcare access, treatment, and health outcomes between groups, i.e., reducing the gap in high-quality care between groups [70].

documents.snippet: Community health workers are increasingly recognized as useful for improving health care and health outcomes for a variety of chronic conditions. Community health workers can provide social support, navigation of health systems and resources, and lay counseling. Title: Medicaid Expansion and Racial and Ethnic Disparities in Access to Health Care: Applying the National Academy of Medicine Definition of Health Care Disparities
Snippet: Since 2014, 32 states implemented Medicaid expansion by removing the categorical criteria for childless adults and by expanding income eligibility to 138% of the federal poverty level (FPL) for all non-elderly adults. Previous studies found that the Affordable Care Act (ACA) Medicaid expansion improved rates of being insured, unmet needs for care due to cost, number of physician visits, and health status among low-income adults. However, a few recent studies focused on the expansion’s effect on racial/ethnic disparities and used the National Academy of Medicine (NAM) disparity approach with a limited set of access measures. This quasi-experimental study examined the effect of Medicaid expansion on racial/ethnic disparities in access to health care for U.S. citizens aged 19 to 64 with income below 138% of the federal poverty line. There were differences across racial/ethnic groups regarding which specific access measures improved. For delayed care and unmet need for care, decreases in racial/ethnic disparities were observed. After the ACA Medicaid expansion, most access outcomes improved for disadvantaged groups, but also for others, with the result that disparities were not significantly reduced.

Title: Medicaid Expansion and Disparity Reduction in Surgical Cancer Care at High Quality Hospitals
Snippet: Background The Affordable Care Act’s (ACA) Medicaid expansion has been heavily debated due to skepticism of Medicaid’s ability to provide high-quality care. Particularly, little is known whether Medicaid expansion improves access to surgical cancer care at high-quality hospitals. To address this question, we examined the effects of the 2001 New York Medicaid expansion, the largest in pre-ACA era, on this disparity measure. Methods We identified 67,685 nonelderly adults from the New York State Inpatient Database who underwent select cancer resections. High-quality hospitals were defined as high-volume hospitals or low-mortality. Disparity was defined as model-adjusted difference in percentage of patients operated at high-quality hospitals by insurance type (Medicaid/uninsured vs. privately insured) or by race (African-American vs. white). Levels of disparity were calculated quarterly for each comparison pair, then analyzed using interrupted time series to evaluate the impact of Medicaid expansion. Results Disparity in access to high-volume hospitals by insurance type was reduced by 0.61 percentage points per quarter following expansion (p=0.003). Medicaid/uninsured beneficiaries had similar access to low-mortality hospitals as the privately insured; no significant change was detected around expansion. Conversely, racial disparity increased by 0.86 percentage points per quarter (p<0.001) in access to high-volume hospitals and by 0.48 percentage points per quarter (p=0.005) in access to low-mortality hospitals following Medicaid expansion. Conclusion Pre-ACA Medicaid expansion reduced the disparity in access to surgical cancer care at high-volume hospitals by payer. However, it was associated with increased racial disparity in access to high-quality hospitals. Addressing racial barriers in access to high-quality hospitals should be prioritized.

Snippet: Background The United States (U.S.) healthcare system consistently underperforms in equity and value compared to peer countries. Socially disadvantaged groups, such as racial and ethnic minorities, refugees, and low-income populations, experience worse access to healthcare and poorer health outcomes. This issue highlights the need for targeted interventions to reduce disparities and improve healthcare quality in both public health and clinical practice. This scoping review aims to map existing literature on interventions that promote healthcare equity and value in the US, focusing on access to healthcare and health outcomes for disadvantaged populations. Methods A scoping review of systematic reviews was conducted to map literature on high-value, equitable healthcare in the U.S. Using the Arksey and O’Malley framework and PRISMA-ScR guidelines, the review focused on systematic reviews of interventions, strategies, and policies promoting healthcare equity and value published between 2018 and 2023 that addressed U.S.-based healthcare. A two-step article selection process and qualitative synthesis of findings were employed. Results The review synthesized 54 studies, comprising mostly systematic reviews, scoping reviews, and meta-analyses. These studies focused on disadvantaged populations, including racial and ethnic minorities, refugees, and low-income groups. Interventions were categorized into four themes: community engagement and outreach (e.g., use of community health workers), culturally-tailored interventions (e.g., language-concordant care), technology adoption (e.g., digital health tools), and policy reforms (e.g., Medicaid expansion). Title: Nursing strategies to address health disparities in genomics-informed care: a scoping review
Snippet: We noted several gaps in the extant research. First, there was a notable lack of intervention and evaluation studies exploring the feasibility and impact of strategies on health and health disparity outcomes. Most of the scholarship was descriptive and in the form of discussion papers. As such, the strategies identified in this review were broad claims and recommendations. Only 4 included papers evaluated specific strategies. 8][49] We were surprised by these results, given the normative calls by nursing leaders to implement evidence-informed strategies to address health equity. 

Second, the majority of the papers did not include a definition of the disparities or inequities under investigation, creating a lack of clarity on how scholars defined the concept. In some instances, inequities were mentioned briefly and broadly. Given this situation, and to help characterize health disparities and equity issues for our scoping review, we categorized them based on our interpretation of factors identified in each paper. Title: Advancing equity and value in United States healthcare: an umbrella review
Snippet: This points to a significant research gap, as interventions need to move beyond grant-funded interventions for socially disadvantaged groups to implementing sustained policies, strategies, and interventions that address longstanding inequities in healthcare access, treatment, and health outcomes between groups, i.e., reducing the gap in high-quality care between groups [70]. 

Although these reviews highlight the impact of certain interventions (e.g., community health workers, cultural sensitivity education, and policy approaches that promote equity-oriented access) and describe ways to repurpose existing strategies to improve health equity, few reviews directly addressed underlying drivers beyond access. 

Ultimately, progress toward equity will require research conducted in partnership with communities that tests interventions addressing structural drivers of inequity, including delivery models grounded in adequately resourced primary care, equity-oriented policies beyond the Affordable Care Act, and explicit accountability mechanisms for equity and value. Advancing equity will also depend on diversifying who shapes the evidence base, ensuring that research priorities, intervention design, and evaluation reflect the perspectives of the populations most affected by including the community as full partners. 

The findings of this review hold important implications for healthcare policy. Policy interventions such as Medicaid expansion have demonstrated significant improvements in access to care and in dental and perinatal health outcomes among disadvantaged populations. These findings suggest the likely adverse impact on equity and value of policies that "unwind" Medicaid and reduce insurance coverage, exposing the risks of separate and unequal subsystems within the fragmented US healthcare system. Gaps in the existing literature suggest a need for research on policies that explicitly address structural inequities, such as universal healthcare access, and the dismantling of systemic barriers like structural racism. Moreover, successful interventions require continuous monitoring and action to ensure that they are inclusive and equitable across all populations. 

Additionally, the review highlights the importance of integrating digital health technologies with equityfocused designs to prevent further widening of health disparities. While technology has the potential to improve access to care, it must be co-designed in partnership with vulnerable populations, as illustrated by PCORI-funded projects, to avoid failure or even reinforcing existing inequities.

Title: Pathways Community Care Coordination in Low Birth Weight Prevention
Snippet: Infant mortality rates are used as an indicator for the health of a community. To prevent infant deaths, mothers need to be healthy, live in a safe environment, and have access to quality care. Reducing low birth weight (LBW) and premature births has been identified as a key strategy to decrease infant mortality [1]. While infant mortality rates in the US have improved over the past decades, they have been stagnant in Ohio. In fact, Ohio ranked second worst for black infant mortality among all states, and fourth worst for overall infant mortality in 2010 [2,3]. Nationally, despite overall improvements, the 2011 Centers for Disease Control (CDC) Health Disparities and Inequalities Report showed that large disparities in infant mortality rates persist [4]. 

Strategies that incorporate the community and directly reach out to women at greatest risk for poor birth outcomes may help communities move towards health equality. Home visiting services are one strategy used to improve birth outcomes and have received increased attention and focus on providing evidence-based services to vulnerable children and families through the Affordable Care Act and the Maternal, Infant, and Early Childhood Home Visiting (MIECHV) program [5]. Although home visiting has been shown to be effective in impacting parent behaviors, child cognitive outcomes and maternal life course, the impact on birth outcomes is not as clearly evident [6,7]. 

The Community Health Access Project (CHAP) is a nonprofit, community based organization that has been providing care coordination services in Richland County, Ohio since 1999. CHAP utilizes community health workers (CHWs) to identify women at risk of having poor birth outcomes, connect them to health and social services, and track each identified issue to a measurable completion. CHAP's intensive home visiting model uses an accountability tool called Pathways [8,9]. A Pathway addresses clearly defined actions towards problem resolution and is not considered complete until a measurable outcome is achieved. One participant may be assigned to many different Pathways depending on the problems identified during the initial interview and subsequent home visits [10]. As in most communities, Richland County had geographic areas of health inequality. CHAP used a mapping strategy to determine the census tracts where the unfavorable birth outcomes were disproportionately occurring.

Title: Rural Health Networks and Care Coordination: Health Care Innovation in Frontier Communities to Improve Patient Outcomes and Reduce Health Care Costs
Snippet: health services in rural communities. 1,2 This embedded case study describes outcomes of implementation of a community care team (CCT) employing collaboration and care coordination to improve patient outcomes and reduce emergency room use in a frontier community, Ely, Minnesota, with a population of 3,450. 3 An original partner in the Minnesota (MN) Health Care Homes project in 2011, the Ely CCT serves Northeastern (NE) Minnesota, a region with higher rates of poor physical and mental health days, poverty, and unemployment than the state and nation. 4,5 Health care access is challenged by distance, two hours from the closest urban area. Concerned organizations, including the clinic, critical access hospital, schools, and mental health organizations, identified community care coordination as their evidence-based strategy to improve health outcomes in their community. [6][7][8] Effectiveness of this strategy in rural communities has not been demonstrated, although projects such as the Vermont Blueprint for Health 9 have led the effort.

Title: Medicaid Expansion and Disparity Reduction in Surgical Cancer Care at High Quality Hospitals
Snippet: Background The Affordable Care Act’s (ACA) Medicaid expansion has been heavily debated due to skepticism of Medicaid’s ability to provide high-quality care. Particularly, little is known whether Medicaid expansion improves access to surgical cancer care at high-quality hospitals. To address this question, we examined the effects of the 2001 New York Medicaid expansion, the largest in pre-ACA era, on this disparity measure. Methods We identified 67,685 nonelderly adults from the New York State Inpatient Database who underwent select cancer resections. High-quality hospitals were defined as high-volume hospitals or low-mortality. Disparity was defined as model-adjusted difference in percentage of patients operated at high-quality hospitals by insurance type (Medicaid/uninsured vs. privately insured) or by race (African-American vs. white). Levels of disparity were calculated quarterly for each comparison pair, then analyzed using interrupted time series to evaluate the impact of Medicaid expansion. Results Disparity in access to high-volume hospitals by insurance type was reduced by 0.61 percentage points per quarter following expansion (p=0.003). Medicaid/uninsured beneficiaries had similar access to low-mortality hospitals as the privately insured; no significant change was detected around expansion. Conversely, racial disparity increased by 0.86 percentage points per quarter (p<0.001) in access to high-volume hospitals and by 0.48 percentage points per quarter (p=0.005) in access to low-mortality hospitals following Medicaid expansion. Conclusion Pre-ACA Medicaid expansion reduced the disparity in access to surgical cancer care at high-volume hospitals by payer. However, it was associated with increased racial disparity in access to high-quality hospitals. Addressing racial barriers in access to high-quality hospitals should be prioritized.
